days.title: Security and Compliance Concepts: Shared Responsibility, Defense in Depth, Zero Trust, Encryption, and GRC

concepts.heading: The Shared Responsibility Model
concepts.body: When a company runs everything in its own datacenter, it is responsible for every part of security, from the building to the data. In the cloud, that responsibility is shared between the cloud provider and the customer, and the split depends on the service type. The provider is always responsible for the physical datacenter, the physical network and the physical hosts. The customer is always responsible for its information and data, the devices that connect, and the accounts and identities of its people. The layers in between move with the service type: in infrastructure as a service (IaaS) the customer patches the operating system of its virtual machines; in platform as a service (PaaS) the provider runs the operating system; in software as a service (SaaS) the provider runs almost the whole application. For example, a company that moves its email to a SaaS service no longer patches mail servers, but it still decides who gets a mailbox and protects its users' accounts.

concepts.heading: Defense in Depth and the CIA Triad
concepts.body: Defense in depth protects information with several layers, so that if one layer fails an attacker still meets the next one instead of reaching the data. The layers usually listed are physical security (locked buildings, badge readers), identity and access (multifactor authentication, role-based access), perimeter (DDoS protection and edge firewalls), network (segmentation and network security groups between resources), compute (patched operating systems, closed ports), application (secure code that rejects bad input) and data (encryption and access controls), which is the innermost layer. The goals of all these layers are summed up as the CIA triad: confidentiality means only authorized people can read the data, integrity means the data is not changed without detection, and availability means systems and data are there when authorized users need them. For example, encrypting a customer file protects confidentiality, a hash of the file protects integrity, and a backup in a second region protects availability.

concepts.heading: The Zero Trust Model
concepts.body: Older security trusted everything inside the corporate network, like a castle with a moat. Zero Trust assumes that nothing is trusted by default, wherever a request comes from, and it rests on three principles. Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize every request using all available signals, such as the user's identity, location, device health, the app being used and unusual behavior. Use least privileged access: give only the access a task needs and only for as long as it is needed, using just-in-time and just-enough-access. Assume breach: design as if an attacker is already inside, so segment access, encrypt end to end and watch for unusual activity to detect attacks quickly. Zero Trust is applied across six areas that produce signals (identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure and networks) plus a seventh, visibility, automation and orchestration, which correlates those signals with SIEM and SOAR tools. For example, an administrator who receives admin rights for two hours only, and must sign in with MFA from a healthy device, is working under Zero Trust.

concepts.heading: Encryption and Hashing
concepts.body: Encryption turns readable data into ciphertext that only someone with the right key can turn back into plain data. Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; it is fast for large amounts of data, but both sides must share the key safely. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys: data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, which solves the problem of sharing a key with strangers and underpins TLS and digital signatures. Data is protected in three states: at rest (stored on disk, protected by storage encryption), in transit (moving across a network, protected by TLS or a VPN) and in use (in memory while processed, protected by confidential computing). Hashing is different: it turns input into a fixed-length value that cannot be turned back into the original. The same input always gives the same hash, so hashes are used to check that files were not changed and to store passwords. Adding a unique random value called a salt to each password before hashing stops attackers from using precomputed tables of common passwords.

concepts.heading: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC)
concepts.body: GRC brings together three ideas that help an organization meet its obligations. Governance is the set of rules, practices and processes used to direct and control the organization, such as who may approve admin access. Risk management means identifying threats, assessing their impact and likelihood, and choosing a response: accept the risk, mitigate it with controls, transfer it to someone else (for example with insurance) or avoid it by changing the process. Compliance means following the laws, regulations and standards that apply because of the industry, the countries involved and the types of data held. Some compliance terms appear often. Data residency is about where data may be stored and moved. Data sovereignty means that data is subject to the laws of the countries where it is collected, held or processed. Data privacy is about handling personal data transparently, with consent, and letting people see, correct or delete their information. For example, a clinic that stores patient records only in its own country is meeting a data residency requirement.

examPoints: A question that asks who is responsible for data, devices, or accounts and identities in the cloud is testing shared responsibility: the customer always keeps these, and the physical datacenter is always the provider's.

A question that describes just-in-time or just-enough admin access is testing the Zero Trust principle use least privileged access; one that describes segmenting and monitoring as if attackers are inside is testing assume breach.
A question that asks how to detect whether a file or password was changed is testing hashing, while one about keeping data unreadable to anyone without a key is testing encryption.

quiz.q: A company wants to be able to tell whether anyone has changed its archived invoice files since they were stored. Which approach mainly protects the integrity of these files?
choices: Encrypting the files with a symmetric key that only the finance team can use
Recording a hash of each file and comparing it with a new hash at a later date
Copying the files to a second region so they stay available during an outage
Placing the storage account behind a perimeter firewall with DDoS protection
quiz.explain: The same input always gives the same hash, so a different hash later shows that a file was changed, which is integrity. Choice A is tempting, but encryption keeps the files confidential; it does not by itself show whether a file was altered.

quiz.q: A company buys a cyber insurance policy so that an insurer pays most of the costs if a ransomware attack occurs. Which risk response is the company using?
choices: Accepting the risk, because the company decides to take no action against it
Avoiding the risk, because the company stops the activity that creates it
Mitigating the risk, because new controls make an attack less likely to occur
Transferring the risk, because another party takes on the financial impact
quiz.explain: Insurance moves the financial impact of the event to another party, which is transferring the risk. Choice C is tempting, but mitigation adds controls that lower the likelihood or impact; insurance only changes who pays.

days.recap: Security in the cloud is shared between provider and customer, built in layers (defense in depth) toward confidentiality, integrity and availability, guided by Zero Trust's verify explicitly, least privilege and assume breach, supported by encryption and hashing, and directed by governance, risk management and compliance.

days.title: Identity Concepts: Identity as the Perimeter, Authentication, Identity Providers, AD DS, and Federation

concepts.heading: Identity as the Primary Security Perimeter
concepts.body: In the past, most work happened on company computers inside the office network, so firewalls at the network edge were the main line of defense. Today people work from home and on the move, use personal phones and tablets, sign in to cloud apps that sit outside the corporate network, and share files with partners and customers. Because access no longer passes through one network boundary, the identity of the person, service or device asking for access has become the main security perimeter. An identity infrastructure rests on four pillars. Administration covers creating and managing identities through their life. Authentication checks that an identity is who it claims to be. Authorization decides what an authenticated identity may access. Auditing records who did what, when and where, so incidents can be investigated. For example, an investigator who needs to know which account opened a payroll file at midnight relies on the auditing pillar.

concepts.heading: Authentication and Authorization
concepts.body: Authentication (often shortened to AuthN) proves who someone is, while authorization (AuthZ) decides what that proven identity is allowed to do. Authentication always comes first. Think of a hotel: showing your passport at the front desk is authentication, and the key card that opens only your room and the gym is authorization. Authentication uses factors from three categories: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone or security key) and something you are (a fingerprint or face). Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires factors from at least two different categories, so a password plus a security question is still only one category and is not MFA. A common exam scenario describes a user who signs in successfully but then sees an access denied message when opening a report; the sign-in shows that authentication worked, so it is authorization that refused the request.

concepts.heading: Identity Providers and Modern Protocols
concepts.body: An identity provider creates, maintains and manages identity information and offers authentication, authorization and auditing services to other applications. Instead of every app keeping its own user list and passwords, apps trust the identity provider. The user signs in once at the identity provider, which issues security tokens that the apps accept. This is what makes single sign-on (SSO) possible: one sign-in gives access to many apps, and disabling one account at the identity provider removes access to all of them when someone leaves. Microsoft Entra ID is an example of a cloud identity provider. Modern identity providers use standard protocols. OpenID Connect (OIDC) handles authentication and returns an ID token that tells the app who the user is. OAuth 2.0 handles authorization and returns an access token that lets an app call an API on the user's behalf. SAML is an older standard that many enterprise web apps still use for SSO.

concepts.heading: Directory Services and Active Directory Domain Services
concepts.body: A directory service is a hierarchical store of information about objects on a network, such as users, groups, computers and printers, together with the services that let people and apps find and use them. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's long-established on-premises directory service. It runs on servers called domain controllers, authenticates users and computers with protocols such as Kerberos and NTLM, and applies settings to computers through Group Policy. For example, when an office worker signs in to a domain-joined Windows PC, a domain controller checks the password and applies the company's desktop settings. AD DS was designed for a world of on-premises networks. It does not natively support modern internet protocols such as OAuth and OpenID Connect, cloud SaaS apps or mobile devices, and remote users usually need a VPN to reach it. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud-based identity and access service that extends these ideas to the cloud, but it is not simply AD DS running in Azure.

concepts.heading: Federation
concepts.body: Federation lets an organization trust identities that another identity provider manages, so users can reach a service with credentials they already have, without a separate account for every service. Federation is built on a trust relationship: the service accepts the security tokens issued by the trusted identity provider. A trust is one-way unless both sides set it up in each direction. If Company A trusts Company B's identity provider, Company B's staff can use their own sign-in to reach Company A's portal, but Company A's staff cannot reach Company B's resources until Company B also trusts Company A. A familiar example is a consumer website that offers sign in with a Google or Microsoft account: the website federates with those social identity providers. In enterprises, Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) is the on-premises Microsoft service that issues tokens from AD DS accounts so cloud services can trust users from the on-premises directory.

examPoints: A question where a user signs in successfully but is refused access to a resource is testing authorization; one that asks how a user proves who they are is testing authentication.
A question that asks whether two factors count as MFA is testing factor categories: the factors must come from different categories (know, have, are), not just be two separate checks.

A question about letting users from another organization or a social account sign in with credentials they already have is testing federation, and remember that a federation trust is one-way unless set up in both directions.

quiz.q: A university has thirty web apps, each with its own sign-in page. It wants students to sign in once and then open every app without entering credentials again. Which concept describes this goal?
choices: Single sign-on through one identity provider whose tokens all of the apps trust
Group Policy applied from a domain controller to every app server on the campus
Data residency rules that keep each student account stored inside one country
Hashing every student password with a salt before storing it in each of the apps
quiz.explain: Single sign-on lets one sign-in at a trusted identity provider give access to many apps through security tokens. Choice B is tempting because domain controllers authenticate users, but Group Policy configures computers; it does not give web apps one shared sign-in.

quiz.q: Which sign-in combination meets the definition of multifactor authentication?
choices: A password together with the answers to two personal security questions
A password together with a PIN code that the user remembers from memory
A password together with an approval on the user's registered phone app
A long passphrase typed twice on two separate sign-in pages of the portal
quiz.explain: The password is something you know and the phone is something you have, so the factors come from two categories. Choice B is tempting because it uses two secrets, but a password and a remembered PIN are both something you know, which is a single category.

days.recap: Identity is now the main security perimeter; authentication proves who you are and authorization decides what you may do, identity providers issue tokens for single sign-on over OIDC, OAuth 2.0 and SAML, AD DS is the on-premises directory service, and federation trusts identities from another provider.

days.title: Microsoft Entra ID and Identity Types: Users, Guests, Devices, Workload Identities, and Hybrid Identity

concepts.heading: What Microsoft Entra ID Is
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service. It lets employees and partners sign in to Microsoft 365, the Azure portal and thousands of SaaS apps, and it lets organizations protect those sign-ins. Every Microsoft 365, Azure or Dynamics 365 subscription already comes with a Microsoft Entra tenant, which is a dedicated instance of Entra ID for one organization, so a company that signs up for Microsoft 365 is already using the Free edition. Paid editions add features: Microsoft Entra ID P1 adds capabilities such as Conditional Access, dynamic groups and password writeback, and Microsoft Entra ID P2 adds Microsoft Entra ID Protection and Privileged Identity Management (PIM is also licensed through Microsoft Entra ID Governance). For legacy apps that need Kerberos, NTLM or LDAP in the cloud, Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides managed domain services so the company does not have to run its own domain controllers in Azure.

concepts.heading: Users, Groups, and Guests
concepts.body: A user identity represents a person. Member users are usually employees of the organization, while guest users come from outside, such as partners, suppliers or consultants. With Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration, a company invites external people to use its apps and files; they sign in with their own work, school or social identity, and they appear as guest user objects in the company's tenant, so the company does not manage their passwords. For public-facing apps used by customers, Microsoft Entra External ID can use a separate external tenant where customers sign up for themselves, for example with an email address or a social account, kept apart from employee identities. Groups collect users so that access can be given once to the whole group: security groups control access to resources, and Microsoft 365 groups add a shared mailbox, calendar and files for collaboration. Group membership can be assigned by hand or, with P1, kept up to date by dynamic rules based on user attributes such as department.

concepts.heading: Device Identities
concepts.body: A device identity is an object in Microsoft Entra ID that represents a phone, tablet or computer, so that the device can be considered in access decisions, for example allowing only healthy, managed devices to open sensitive apps. There are three ways for a device to get an identity. Microsoft Entra registered is for personal (bring your own device) and mobile devices: the user adds a work account to their own phone or laptop. Microsoft Entra joined is for organization-owned Windows devices whose users sign in with their work account, with no on-premises Active Directory needed. Microsoft Entra hybrid joined is for organization-owned Windows devices that are joined to on-premises Active Directory and also registered in Microsoft Entra ID. For example, a nurse who adds her work account to her own iPhone registers it, while the hospital's own laptops are Entra joined. Device identities work together with device management tools such as Microsoft Intune, which reports whether a device is compliant.

concepts.heading: Workload Identities
concepts.body: A workload identity is an identity given to software, such as an application, a script or a service, rather than to a person. Microsoft Entra has three kinds. An application object is the global definition of an app, created when the app is registered. A service principal is the local instance of that app in a particular tenant; it defines what the app can do in that tenant and who can use it, so a multitenant app has one application object but a service principal in every tenant that uses it. A managed identity is a special service principal that Azure creates and manages for an Azure resource, so the app needs no stored password, key or certificate. A system-assigned managed identity belongs to one resource and is deleted with it. A user-assigned managed identity is created on its own, can be shared by several resources and keeps existing when those resources are deleted. For example, a web app in Azure App Service can use its managed identity to read secrets from Azure Key Vault without any credentials in its code.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Identity
concepts.body: Many organizations keep on-premises Active Directory and also use cloud apps. Hybrid identity gives users one common identity across both. Synchronization copies users and groups from on-premises AD into Microsoft Entra ID, using either Microsoft Entra Connect Sync, a server-based tool, or Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync, which uses lightweight agents with configuration managed from the cloud and can sync disconnected forests. Users then sign in to the cloud by one of three methods. Password hash synchronization (PHS) syncs a hash of the password hash to the cloud, so Entra ID checks the password itself; it is the simplest option with the least on-premises infrastructure. Pass-through authentication (PTA) sends the password check to agents on premises, so on-premises account states and logon hours are enforced at sign-in. Federation hands sign-in to a separate system such as AD FS, used when sign-in must rely on an on-premises or third-party method that Entra ID does not support. For example, a small firm with one office usually picks password hash synchronization.

examPoints: A question about external partners using their own identities to reach your apps is testing B2B collaboration and guest users; one about customers signing up themselves to a public app is testing External ID with an external tenant.

A question about an Azure app reaching another Azure service without any stored secret is testing managed identities: system-assigned for one resource, user-assigned for an identity shared by several resources.

A question about a personal phone getting a device identity is testing Microsoft Entra registered; company Windows devices are Entra joined, or hybrid joined when they are also joined to on-premises AD.

quiz.q: A company wants its on-premises users to sign in to Microsoft 365 with their usual password. It must keep password checks on premises, and an account locked on premises must not be able to sign in to the cloud. Which method fits?
choices: Password hash synchronization, which lets Microsoft Entra ID check the password
Microsoft Entra Domain Services, which runs managed domain controllers in Azure
Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration, which invites each user as a guest account
Pass-through authentication, which sends password checks to on-premises agents
quiz.explain: Pass-through authentication validates passwords on premises, so on-premises account states such as lockout apply at sign-in. Choice A is tempting because it is the simplest hybrid method, but with password hash synchronization the password is checked in the cloud, which the company does not want.

quiz.q: Six Azure virtual machines run a nightly job that needs the same access to one storage account. The machines are often rebuilt, and the identity should survive the rebuilds. Which identity fits?
choices: A system-assigned managed identity enabled separately on each of the machines
A user-assigned managed identity created once and assigned to all the machines
A guest user account invited into the tenant and shared by all of the machines
A password stored in the job script and rotated by hand by the operations team
quiz.explain: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone resource that several machines can share, and it keeps existing when the machines are deleted. Choice A is tempting, but a system-assigned identity belongs to one resource and is deleted with it, so each rebuild would create a new identity.

days.recap: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service for users, guests, groups, devices and workload identities such as service principals and managed identities, and hybrid identity syncs on-premises AD with Connect Sync or Cloud Sync and signs users in with password hash sync, pass-through authentication or federation.

days.title: Authentication in Microsoft Entra: Methods, Passwordless, MFA, SSPR, Password Protection, and Security Defaults

concepts.heading: Authentication Methods in Microsoft Entra ID
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID supports many ways to prove identity, and they differ in security and convenience. Passwords are the most common but the weakest, because they can be guessed, reused or stolen. Phone-based methods send a code by SMS or a voice call; they are better than a password alone, but Microsoft recommends moving users away from them toward stronger methods. Microsoft Authenticator is a free phone app that can approve sign-in notifications, show one-time codes and hold passkeys for passwordless sign-in. OATH tokens are hardware or software tokens that display a time-based code. Certificate-based authentication lets users sign in with X.509 certificates, such as smart cards from an organization's own PKI, without needing AD FS. A Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode that an admin issues so a user can sign in to register a passwordless method, for example on a new hire's first day.

concepts.heading: Passwordless and Phishing-Resistant Methods
concepts.body: Passwordless methods replace the password with something you have, combined with a biometric or PIN, which makes sign-in both easier and safer. Windows Hello for Business uses a PIN, face or fingerprint on a Windows device; the PIN only unlocks a private key that is tied to that device, so the PIN never travels over the network and is useless on any other device. Passkeys (FIDO2) work the same way: the private key stays on the device or security key, and the service only stores the public key, so there is no reusable secret to steal. Passkeys can be device-bound, such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys in Microsoft Authenticator, or synced through a cloud provider; when a key must never leave the hardware, choose a device-bound passkey. Windows Hello for Business, passkeys and certificate-based authentication are phishing-resistant, because a fake website cannot capture anything it could replay. Codes typed or approved by the user are not phishing-resistant.

concepts.heading: Multifactor Authentication
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication (MFA) asks for two or more factors from different categories: something you know, something you have and something you are. A password plus an approval in Microsoft Authenticator is MFA because the phone is something you have. MFA greatly reduces the chance that a stolen password alone lets an attacker in. Some methods count as more than one factor on their own: a passkey on a phone unlocked with a fingerprint combines something you have with something you are, so it satisfies MFA without any password. Organizations decide when MFA is required, for example on every sign-in through security defaults, or only in certain situations, such as sign-ins from outside the office, through Conditional Access policies. For example, a sales team that signs in from hotels and airports might be asked for MFA on each sign-in from an unknown network, while staff in the office see fewer prompts.

concepts.heading: Self-Service Password Reset and Password Protection
concepts.body: Self-service password reset (SSPR) lets users reset a forgotten password or unlock their account without calling the help desk, after proving who they are with registered methods such as Authenticator notifications or codes, SMS, a voice call or an email code. Admins choose whether one or two methods are needed, but accounts that hold Microsoft Entra administrator roles always need two. For hybrid users, password writeback writes the new cloud password back to on-premises Active Directory so it works everywhere at once. Microsoft Entra Password Protection stops users from choosing weak passwords. A global banned password list, built from Microsoft's telemetry, applies automatically to every user. A custom banned password list adds terms specific to the organization, such as its brand names or city. Installing the Password Protection proxy and DC agent extends these checks to password changes on on-premises domain controllers. Smart lockout, which is always on, locks out attackers who keep guessing passwords while trying to let the real user keep signing in.

concepts.heading: Security Defaults
concepts.body: Security defaults are a set of preconfigured security settings that Microsoft provides at no extra cost to help protect organizations against common identity attacks such as password spray and phishing. When security defaults are on, all users must register for MFA, administrators must use MFA, users are asked for MFA when needed, and legacy authentication protocols, which cannot perform MFA, are blocked. Security defaults are switched on for new tenants at creation and are aimed at organizations that want good protection but do not know where to start, and especially at organizations using the Free edition of Microsoft Entra ID. They are all-or-nothing: you cannot choose which users or apps they cover. Organizations that need more control, for example requiring MFA only for certain apps or locations, use Conditional Access policies instead, which need Microsoft Entra ID P1. Security defaults and Conditional Access policies are not used together; an organization turns security defaults off when it moves to Conditional Access.

examPoints: A question that asks for phishing-resistant or passwordless sign-in is testing Windows Hello for Business, passkeys (FIDO2) or certificate-based authentication; SMS and voice codes are not phishing-resistant.
A question about users resetting their own forgotten passwords is testing SSPR; if the new password must also work on premises, the answer adds password writeback.

A question about a Free-tier tenant that wants baseline MFA and blocked legacy authentication with no custom policies is testing security defaults; one that needs rules for specific users, apps or locations is testing Conditional Access.

quiz.q: A company named Contoso finds that many staff choose passwords such as Contoso2026 and Contoso!1. It wants these rejected whenever users change or reset passwords. What should it configure?
choices: A custom banned password list in Password Protection that holds the brand name
Smart lockout with a shorter lockout period after each failed sign-in to the tenant
A Temporary Access Pass for every user so that no one needs to type a password
Self-service password reset that requires two verification methods for each user
quiz.explain: The custom banned password list adds organization-specific terms, such as the brand name, to the checks made when passwords are changed or reset. Choice B is tempting because it fights password attacks, but smart lockout blocks repeated guessing; it does not reject weak passwords that users choose.

quiz.q: A user asks why the short PIN she uses with Windows Hello for Business is safer than her long domain password. Which statement explains it?
choices: The PIN is sent to Microsoft Entra ID with stronger encryption than a password is
The PIN is changed automatically every day, so a stolen PIN soon stops working
The PIN only unlocks a private key on her device and never leaves the device
The PIN is checked against the global banned list more strictly than a password is
quiz.explain: A Windows Hello for Business PIN unlocks a key bound to that device, so it is never sent over the network and is useless anywhere else. Choice A is tempting, but the PIN is not sent to the service at all; only the device's key is used to sign the sign-in.

days.recap: Microsoft Entra ID supports methods from passwords and SMS to Authenticator, certificates and phishing-resistant passwordless options such as Windows Hello for Business and passkeys, adds MFA, lets users fix passwords with SSPR, blocks weak passwords with Password Protection, and gives Free tenants baseline protection with security defaults.

days.title: Access Management: Conditional Access, Microsoft Entra Roles, and Azure RBAC

concepts.heading: What Conditional Access Does
concepts.body: Conditional Access is the Microsoft Entra feature that brings signals together, makes a decision and enforces organizational policy. It works like a set of if-then statements: if a user wants to reach a resource under certain conditions, then they must complete an action or are blocked. It is a key part of Zero Trust because it verifies explicitly on every sign-in instead of trusting the network. Conditional Access is evaluated after the user completes the first authentication factor, so it is not a defense against network floods such as DDoS attacks. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P1. For example, a company can write a policy that says: if anyone in the finance group opens the payroll app from outside the office, then require MFA. Before a new policy is enforced, admins can run it in report-only mode, which records what the policy would have done on real sign-ins without blocking anyone, so mistakes are found before they lock users out.

concepts.heading: Signals and Conditions
concepts.body: Signals are the information Conditional Access evaluates before it decides. The main signals are the user or group making the request, including whether they are a guest; the location, defined by IP address ranges or countries; the device, such as its platform and whether it is marked compliant by Intune; the application being opened; and risk. Risk comes from Microsoft Entra ID Protection, which rates how likely it is that a sign-in or a user account is compromised; using risk in policies needs P2. A policy is assigned to users and target resources, and conditions narrow when it applies, for example only to sign-ins from outside named locations or only from certain device platforms. Another condition is the client app type: older clients that use legacy authentication cannot complete MFA, so Microsoft recommends a Conditional Access policy that blocks legacy authentication. For example, a policy can target all users, all cloud apps and the legacy authentication client types, with the decision block access.

concepts.heading: Access Decisions: Grant and Session Controls
concepts.body: After evaluating signals, Conditional Access reaches a decision. Block access is the most restrictive decision and stops the sign-in. Grant access lets the user in, usually only after meeting one or more requirements, such as requiring multifactor authentication, requiring an authentication strength (for example phishing-resistant MFA), requiring the device to be marked as compliant, requiring a Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device, requiring an app protection policy, or requiring a password change for a risky user. When several grant controls are selected, the admin chooses require all the selected controls (an AND) or require one of the selected controls (an OR). Session controls shape the experience after access is granted. Sign-in frequency sets how long a user can stay signed in before signing in again, persistent browser session decides whether users stay signed in after closing the browser, and Conditional Access App Control routes the session through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps for real-time monitoring, such as blocking downloads of sensitive files on unmanaged devices.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra Roles
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra roles control who can manage Microsoft Entra resources such as users, groups, applications and tenant settings. They are built on role-based access control: a role assignment combines a security principal (who), a role definition (what they can do) and a scope (where). Built-in roles have fixed permissions. Global Administrator can manage nearly everything in the tenant, User Administrator manages users and groups, Helpdesk Administrator resets passwords for non-administrators and other Helpdesk Administrators, and Billing Administrator handles purchases and subscriptions. When no built-in role fits, organizations can create custom roles that include only the permissions they choose; each user with a custom role assignment needs a Microsoft Entra ID P1 license. Roles can be scoped to the whole tenant, to an administrative unit such as one country's users, or to a single object such as one app registration. Following least privilege, Microsoft recommends giving each person the most specific role for their task and keeping the number of Global Administrators as small as possible.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra Roles Versus Azure RBAC
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra roles and Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) are separate systems. Microsoft Entra roles manage directory objects, such as users, groups, passwords and app registrations. Azure RBAC manages access to Azure resources, such as virtual machines, storage accounts and networks. Azure RBAC has four fundamental built-in roles: Owner can manage everything and assign access to others, Contributor can create and manage all resources but cannot grant access, Reader can only view resources, and User Access Administrator can only manage access for others. Azure RBAC roles are assigned at a scope in the hierarchy of management group, subscription, resource group or single resource, and assignments are inherited by everything below. For least privilege, choose the most specific role and the narrowest scope that does the job. For example, a developer who manages virtual machines in one project gets Virtual Machine Contributor on that project's resource group, while a help desk agent who only resets passwords gets the Helpdesk Administrator Entra role and no Azure role.

examPoints: A question phrased as if this user, location, device, app or risk, then require MFA or block is testing Conditional Access; report-only mode tests a new policy on real sign-ins without enforcing it.

A question that asks which items are signals and which are decisions is testing the Conditional Access model: users, locations, devices, apps and risk go in; block, grant with requirements, and session controls come out.
A question about managing users, groups or passwords is testing Microsoft Entra roles, while one about managing virtual machines, storage or other Azure resources at a scope is testing Azure RBAC.

quiz.q: Contractors may open a company's cloud document app from their own laptops, but the company wants downloads of sensitive files blocked during those sessions. Which Conditional Access capability supports this?
choices: The grant control require multifactor authentication on every contractor sign-in
The session control Conditional Access App Control with Defender for Cloud Apps
The location condition that limits the app to sign-ins from the office IP ranges
The report-only mode that records which sign-ins a new policy would have blocked
quiz.explain: Conditional Access App Control routes the session through Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, which can monitor it and block downloads in real time. Choice A is tempting, but MFA only checks the sign-in; it cannot control what the user does inside the session.

quiz.q: An engineer must create, change and delete every resource in an Azure subscription, but must not be able to give other people access to those resources. Which built-in role fits exactly?
choices: Owner, assigned at the scope of the subscription that holds the resources
Global Administrator, assigned in the Microsoft Entra tenant of the company
User Access Administrator, assigned at the scope of the same subscription
Contributor, assigned at the scope of the subscription with the resources
quiz.explain: Contributor can manage all resources at its scope but cannot assign roles to others. Choice A is tempting because Owner also manages every resource, but Owner can grant access too, which breaks the requirement.

days.recap: Conditional Access turns signals such as user, location, device, app and risk into decisions to block or grant with requirements and session controls, Microsoft Entra roles manage directory objects such as users and groups, and Azure RBAC manages Azure resources with roles assigned at a scope.

days.title: Identity Protection and Governance: ID Governance, Entitlement Management, Access Reviews, Lifecycle Workflows, PIM, and ID Protection

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra ID Governance
concepts.body: Identity governance means making sure that the right people have the right access to the right resources, and that this stays true over time as people join, change jobs and leave. Without governance, access tends to pile up: an employee who has moved through three departments may still hold access from all of them, which breaks least privilege and creates risk. Microsoft Entra ID Governance brings together the tools that manage this identity lifecycle and access lifecycle: entitlement management to request and grant access, access reviews to confirm it is still needed, lifecycle workflows to automate joiner, mover and leaver tasks, and Privileged Identity Management to control admin rights. It also keeps an audit trail, so the organization can show auditors who had access, who approved it and when it was removed. For example, a bank that must prove every quarter that only current staff can open its loan system uses these governance tools rather than spreadsheets and email.

concepts.heading: Entitlement Management and Access Reviews
concepts.body: Entitlement management lets an organization bundle the access a role needs into an access package, which can contain groups, apps and SharePoint Online sites. Policies on the package decide who can request it, who must approve (for example the user's manager), and when the access expires. Users ask for the package themselves through the My Access portal, so they get everything at once instead of filing several tickets. Access packages also work for people outside the company: with connected organizations, users from a partner or supplier can request access, are added to the directory as guests when approved, and are removed when their access ends. Access reviews let owners or managers regularly confirm who still needs access to groups, apps, access packages or privileged roles. A review can run on a schedule, such as every quarter, and access that reviewers do not confirm can be removed automatically. For example, a team owner can be asked every three months to confirm which guest users still need to be in the team's group.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Workflows
concepts.body: Lifecycle workflows automate the routine identity tasks tied to joiner, mover and leaver events. A workflow has a trigger, such as a number of days before or after the employee hire date or the employee leave date stored on the user's account, and a list of tasks to run. Joiner tasks can include generating a Temporary Access Pass and emailing it to the new hire's manager before the first day, adding the user to groups, or sending a welcome email. Leaver tasks can include disabling the account, removing the user from all groups and Teams, and later deleting the account. Each run is logged, so there is a history for auditors. Lifecycle workflows are different from access reviews: lifecycle workflows react automatically to an event in a person's employment, while access reviews ask people to recertify existing access at regular intervals. For example, a company that sometimes forgets to remove group memberships when staff leave can use a leaver workflow that runs on each person's last day.

concepts.heading: Privileged Identity Management
concepts.body: Privileged Identity Management (PIM) manages, controls and monitors access to important resources, putting the Zero Trust idea of least privilege into practice for admin rights. Instead of holding a powerful role all the time, a user can be made eligible for it. An eligible user has no rights until they activate the role, and activation can require MFA, a business justification and approval from a chosen person, after which the role expires automatically after a set time. This is just-in-time access. An active assignment, by contrast, is always on. Assignments can also be time-bound, with a start and end date, for example for a consultant who needs a role only for a three-month project. PIM works for Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles such as Owner on a subscription, and groups. It sends notifications when roles are activated, supports access reviews of who holds roles, and keeps an audit history. Using PIM requires Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance licenses.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra ID Protection
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID Protection uses Microsoft's very large set of signals to detect identity-based risks, and it can respond automatically. It calculates two kinds of risk. Sign-in risk is the probability that a particular sign-in was not made by the account's owner; detections include sign-ins from anonymous IP addresses, atypical travel and unfamiliar sign-in properties. User risk is the probability that the account itself has been compromised; detections include leaked credentials, found when a user's name and password appear in a public breach, and unusual account behavior. Risk feeds into Conditional Access, where a sign-in risk policy can require MFA so the real user can prove themselves, and a user risk policy can require a secure password change, letting users fix the problem without help desk calls. Analysts investigate in the risky users, risky sign-ins and risk detections reports, and the data can be exported to a SIEM such as Microsoft Sentinel. Risk-based policies need Microsoft Entra ID P2.

examPoints: A question about a bundle of groups, apps and sites that users request, managers approve and that expires is testing entitlement management access packages; regular recertification of who still needs access is testing access reviews.

A question where an admin must activate a role with MFA, justification or approval, and the role expires afterwards, is testing Privileged Identity Management and the difference between eligible and active assignments.
A question about leaked credentials is testing user risk, while one about an anonymous IP address or atypical travel is testing sign-in risk in Microsoft Entra ID Protection.

quiz.q: When an employee's leave date arrives, a company wants the account disabled and removed from all groups automatically, with a history kept for auditors. Which capability fits?
choices: Access reviews that ask each manager every quarter to confirm their team's access
Microsoft Entra ID Protection that raises the user risk of the departing account
Lifecycle workflows that run leaver tasks triggered by the employee's leave date
Privileged Identity Management that sets every role of the employee to eligible
quiz.explain: Lifecycle workflows run joiner and leaver tasks automatically from dates such as the leave date and log each run. Choice A is tempting because access reviews also remove access, but they run on a schedule and depend on reviewers, not on the employee's leave date.

quiz.q: Microsoft Entra ID Protection reports that a user's password has appeared in a public breach. Which policy lets the user fix the problem without calling the help desk?
choices: A user risk policy in Conditional Access that requires a secure password change
A sign-in risk policy in Conditional Access that blocks all sign-ins from the user
An access review that asks the user's manager to confirm the user's group access
A PIM eligible assignment that requires approval before the user can sign in again
quiz.explain: Leaked credentials raise user risk, and a user risk policy that requires a secure password change lets the user remediate it themselves. Choice B is tempting because it uses a risk policy, but blocking stops the user completely, and leaked credentials are a user risk, not a sign-in risk.

days.recap: Microsoft Entra ID Governance keeps the right access over time with entitlement management access packages, access reviews and lifecycle workflows, Privileged Identity Management makes admin rights just in time with approval and expiry, and ID Protection detects sign-in risk and user risk and remediates them through Conditional Access.

days.title: Core Infrastructure Security in Azure: DDoS Protection, Azure Firewall, WAF, NSGs, Bastion, and Key Vault

concepts.heading: Azure DDoS Protection
concepts.body: A distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack floods a service with traffic from many sources so that real users cannot reach it. Every Azure service with a public IP address gets DDoS infrastructure protection by default at no additional cost, which defends against common network-layer attacks on the platform. For stronger protection tuned to your own resources, Azure DDoS Protection offers two tiers. DDoS Network Protection is enabled through a DDoS protection plan on virtual networks; one plan can cover virtual networks in many subscriptions under the same tenant. It provides always-on monitoring, adaptive tuning to your traffic, automatic mitigation, alerts and reports, and adds access to the DDoS rapid response team and cost protection for scale-out during a documented attack. DDoS IP Protection is enabled directly on individual public IP addresses with no plan, and it has the same core mitigation but without rapid response or cost protection. DDoS Protection works at network layers 3 and 4, so web application attacks at layer 7 need a WAF as well.

concepts.heading: Azure Firewall
concepts.body: Azure Firewall is a managed, cloud-based network security service that protects resources in Azure virtual networks. It is a stateful firewall as a service with built-in high availability and scaling, usually placed in a central hub virtual network so that traffic from many spoke networks passes through it. Besides network rules on IP addresses, ports and protocols, it can filter outbound traffic by fully qualified domain names (for example, allowing only a software update site), translate addresses with SNAT and DNAT, and use threat intelligence from Microsoft to alert on or deny traffic to known malicious addresses and domains. Every allowed and denied connection can be logged. Azure Firewall comes in three SKUs: Basic for small businesses, where threat intelligence can only alert; Standard, which can alert and deny; and Premium, which adds TLS inspection and signature-based intrusion detection and prevention (IDPS) for sensitive workloads such as payment processing.

concepts.heading: Web Application Firewall
concepts.body: A web application firewall (WAF) protects web applications from common exploits at layer 7, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, so the app is protected before developers fix every vulnerable page. Azure Web Application Firewall uses managed rule sets that Microsoft keeps up to date, and admins can add custom rules, for example geo-filtering to block requests from countries the business does not serve, or rate limits. WAF is not a separate appliance; it runs on Azure services that deliver web traffic. WAF on Azure Front Door filters requests at Microsoft's global network edge, close to users and attackers, before traffic reaches your network. WAF on Azure Application Gateway filters requests regionally, in front of web apps in a virtual network. A WAF runs in detection mode, which only logs matching requests, or prevention mode, which blocks them; Microsoft suggests starting new deployments in detection mode, tuning rules from the logs, and then switching to prevention. For multilayered protection, combine DDoS Protection for network floods with a WAF for web attacks.

concepts.heading: Segmentation and Network Security Groups
concepts.body: Segmentation divides a network into smaller zones so that an attacker who compromises one system cannot freely reach everything else, which supports the Zero Trust idea of assume breach. In Azure, separate virtual networks are isolated from each other by default and only talk when connected deliberately, for example with virtual network peering. Inside one virtual network, subnets organize resources, but Azure routes traffic between subnets by default, so filtering is still needed. Network security groups (NSGs) filter traffic to and from resources by source, destination, port and protocol. Each rule has a priority, and rules are processed from the lowest number up; the first matching rule decides. A new NSG has default rules that allow traffic inside the virtual network and deny other inbound traffic from the internet until an allow rule is added. An NSG can be attached to a subnet, a network interface or both; inbound traffic must be allowed by both. Application security groups let rules name groups of VMs by role, such as web servers, instead of IP addresses.

concepts.heading: Azure Bastion and Azure Key Vault
concepts.body: Administrators often need RDP or SSH access to virtual machines, but opening those ports to the internet invites attacks. Azure Bastion is a fully managed service that provides RDP and SSH connections over TLS from the Azure portal or a native client, so the VMs need no public IP address, no agent and no exposed management ports, and the team does not run its own jump box. Its SKUs range from Developer, a free shared option for test VMs, through Basic and Standard, to Premium, which adds session recording for compliance. Azure Key Vault is a cloud service that securely stores and controls access to secrets (such as connection strings and API keys), encryption keys and certificates, so they stay out of code and configuration files. Callers authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID, often through a managed identity, and are authorized with Azure RBAC or access policies, and access can be logged. The Standard tier protects keys with software, while the Premium tier adds HSM-protected keys. Soft delete makes deleted items recoverable, and purge protection stops anyone from permanently removing them before the retention period ends.

examPoints: A question about network floods is testing Azure DDoS Protection, while one about SQL injection or cross-site scripting is testing a web application firewall; together they give multilayered protection for web apps.

A question about central, stateful control of traffic with FQDN rules or threat intelligence is testing Azure Firewall, while one about simple allow and deny rules by port and IP near a subnet or VM is testing network security groups.
A question about RDP or SSH to VMs without public IP addresses is testing Azure Bastion, and one about keeping secrets, keys and certificates out of code is testing Azure Key Vault.

quiz.q: A network security group has two inbound rules: priority 300 allows TCP port 22 from the admin network, and priority 150 denies TCP port 22 from any source. What happens to SSH traffic from the admin network?
choices: It is allowed, because allow rules are always processed before any deny rules
It is allowed, because a rule with a specific source overrides a rule for any source
It is denied only if the virtual machine's network interface has no NSG of its own
It is denied, because the rule with priority 150 is processed first and matches it
quiz.explain: NSG rules are processed from the lowest priority number up, and the first match decides, so the deny rule at 150 wins. Choice B is tempting because the allow rule is more specific, but NSGs use priority order, not how specific a rule is.

quiz.q: A company wants its public web app protected from web exploits at Microsoft's global network edge, before requests reach its virtual networks in any region. What should it use?
choices: Azure Firewall Premium in a hub virtual network that inspects all inbound web traffic
Azure Web Application Firewall on Azure Front Door, filtering requests at the edge
Azure DDoS Network Protection enabled through a plan on each virtual network
Network security groups on each web subnet that deny port 80 from the internet
quiz.explain: WAF on Azure Front Door blocks web exploits at Microsoft's global edge, before traffic enters your networks. Choice A is tempting because Premium inspects traffic deeply, but Azure Firewall runs inside a virtual network, not at the global edge, and it is a network firewall rather than a WAF for web exploits.

days.recap: Core Azure infrastructure security layers DDoS Protection against network floods, Azure Firewall for central stateful filtering, a WAF on Front Door or Application Gateway against web exploits, segmentation with virtual networks and NSGs, Azure Bastion for RDP and SSH without public IPs, and Azure Key Vault for secrets, keys and certificates.

days.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud: CSPM, Secure Score, and Workload Protection

concepts.heading: Defender for Cloud as a CNAPP
concepts.body: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP): one service that protects an application from the code to the running workload. It covers Azure, other clouds such as AWS and Google Cloud, and on-premises machines. Learn describes three pillars. DevSecOps brings security into development pipelines. Cloud security posture management (CSPM) checks whether resources are configured securely. The cloud workload protection platform (CWPP) detects attacks against running workloads and raises security alerts. A simple way to keep them apart: DevSecOps finds problems before deployment, CSPM finds weaknesses in what is deployed, and CWPP finds someone actively attacking it. For example, a secret committed to a repository is a DevSecOps finding, a storage account open to every network is a CSPM finding, and a suspicious access attempt against that account is a CWPP alert.

concepts.heading: Policies, Standards, and Recommendations
concepts.body: Defender for Cloud decides what to tell you to fix through a chain of objects. A security policy says how resources are evaluated and contains security standards. A standard is a set of controls with assessment logic; it can be a security benchmark, a regulatory compliance standard or a custom standard you write. When you turn Defender for Cloud on, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) is applied by default to Azure subscriptions, AWS accounts and GCP projects, so assessment starts with no setup. Resources are assessed continuously, and each time a resource fails a control, Defender for Cloud creates a security recommendation. A recommendation describes the issue, gives remediation steps, and lists the affected resources, severity and risk factors. For example, an MCSB control says storage accounts should restrict network access, so an account open to all networks becomes a recommendation to restrict it.

concepts.heading: The Secure Score
concepts.body: The secure score rolls the findings of the recommendations into one value, shown as a percentage: the higher the score, the lower the identified risk. Recommendations are grouped into security controls such as Secure management ports, each worth a maximum number of points. A resource earns a control's points only when it passes every recommendation in that control, so fixing one of two open findings on a VM does not move the score. Only built-in MCSB recommendations count, and recommendations marked Preview are left out until they become generally available. Learn names two ways to improve the score: remediate recommendations, manually or with Fix where offered, and use Enforce or Deny so that new resources are fixed automatically or blocked when they would repeat the weakness. Alerts and access permissions do not change the score, because it measures configuration, not attacks.

concepts.heading: Foundational CSPM and Defender CSPM
concepts.body: Posture management comes in two levels. Foundational CSPM is free and turns on automatically for every onboarded subscription or account. It includes asset discovery, continuous assessment, MCSB recommendations, the secure score and multicloud coverage of Azure, AWS and GCP. The paid Defender CSPM plan adds advanced tools. Attack path analysis shows how separate weaknesses, such as an internet-exposed VM with a vulnerability that can reach a storage account with customer data, chain into a route an attacker could follow. The cloud security explorer queries the cloud security graph. Governance assigns recommendations to resource owners with due dates and tracks progress. The regulatory compliance dashboard shows how resources meet the controls of standards; MCSB is assigned by default, and adding further standards such as PCI DSS or ISO 27001 needs at least one paid plan. Those results also appear in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager.

concepts.heading: Workload Protection and DevSecOps
concepts.body: Workload protection is delivered through Defender plans, one per resource type, and each plan adds threat detection and security alerts for that type. Defender for Servers protects Windows and Linux machines in Azure, AWS, GCP and on premises, integrates Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and adds features such as just-in-time VM access, file integrity monitoring and vulnerability assessment. Defender for Storage scans uploaded blobs for malware, detects unusual access and spots misuse of shared access signature tokens. Other plans cover databases, containers, App Service, Key Vault, Resource Manager and APIs. DevSecOps, often called shift left, connects GitHub, Azure DevOps and GitLab to Defender for Cloud so security teams see findings across pipelines, such as infrastructure as code misconfigurations and exposed secrets, and can fix them in the code that creates the resource.

examPoints: A question that contrasts a misconfigured resource with an attack in progress is testing CSPM, which gives recommendations and the secure score, versus workload protection plans, which raise security alerts.

A question that names attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, governance with due dates or added standards such as PCI DSS is testing the paid Defender CSPM plan rather than free Foundational CSPM.
A question that asks why fixing a recommendation did not raise the secure score usually turns on other open recommendations in the same control or on a recommendation still in preview.

quiz.q: Which of these findings comes from the workload protection (CWPP) side of Microsoft Defender for Cloud rather than from posture management?
choices: A recommendation that a storage account should restrict access from public networks
A lower secure score after a new subscription is onboarded without any hardening
A security alert that a suspicious process tried to run on a protected virtual machine
A failed ISO 27001 control shown on the regulatory compliance dashboard in the portal
quiz.explain: Workload protection comes from Defender plans such as Defender for Servers, which watch running workloads and raise security alerts when something suspicious happens. Choice A is tempting because it describes a real risk, but a configuration weakness reported as a recommendation is posture management (CSPM), not workload protection.

quiz.q: A team keeps application secrets in Azure Key Vault and wants Defender for Cloud to alert it when an unusual application or location accesses those vaults. What should it turn on?
choices: The Defender for Key Vault plan, which adds threat detection for unusual vault access
Foundational CSPM, which is free and raises alerts for every resource type by default
The regulatory compliance dashboard with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark
The secure score, which raises an alert whenever a vault is opened from outside
quiz.explain: Threat alerts come from workload protection plans, and Defender for Key Vault is the plan built to detect unusual access to key vaults. Choice B is tempting because Foundational CSPM is on by default, but it provides recommendations and the secure score, not threat alerts.

days.recap: Defender for Cloud is a CNAPP: DevSecOps fixes code, CSPM turns failed MCSB controls into recommendations and a secure score (Defender CSPM adds attack paths, governance and more standards), and Defender plans protect workloads with alerts.

days.title: Microsoft Sentinel: SIEM, SOAR, Detection, and Response

concepts.heading: SIEM, SOAR, and Where Sentinel Runs
concepts.body: A security information and event management (SIEM) system collects logs from the whole estate, such as firewalls, servers, identity systems and applications, correlates them to find patterns that point to a threat, raises alerts and groups related alerts into incidents. An event that looks harmless alone, like a late-night sign-in, becomes significant next to a large download of sensitive files. Security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) takes those alerts and runs automated workflows: orchestration connects tools so they work together, and automation runs repetitive response steps without manual effort. SIEM gives visibility; SOAR gives speed. Microsoft Sentinel is both a cloud-native SIEM and a SOAR platform, built on a Log Analytics workspace. It is generally available in the Microsoft Defender portal, and Learn states that after March 31, 2027 it will no longer be supported in the Azure portal, so plan to use it in the Defender portal.

concepts.heading: Bringing Data In
concepts.body: Sentinel is only as useful as the data it receives, and data connectors bring that data in. Microsoft services such as Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Activity and Microsoft Defender XDR connect service to service. Non-Microsoft products often send Syslog or Common Event Format (CEF) messages, which the Azure Monitor Agent collects, either on the device itself or on a Linux log forwarder, and writes to the workspace. Other sources use REST APIs, the Codeless Connector Framework or the Logs Ingestion API. Connectors usually arrive in solutions from the Content hub, which package a connector with related workbooks, analytics rule templates, hunting queries and playbooks for one product or scenario. Watchlists add your own context, such as lists of terminated employees, service accounts or high-value servers, so rules and hunting queries can check events against them.

concepts.heading: Detection: Analytics Rules and Incidents
concepts.body: Analytics rules query the collected data regularly to discover threats. Scheduled rules are the most common: a Kusto Query Language (KQL) query runs at a set interval over a lookback period, and an alert is produced when results pass a threshold. Near-real-time (NRT) rules are a limited kind of scheduled rule that runs once every minute, for events where minutes matter. Anomaly rules use machine learning to build a baseline and write deviations to an Anomalies table instead of raising alerts. Alerts name the entities involved, such as users, devices and IP addresses, and Sentinel correlates related alerts into incidents. An incident is the case file an analyst works: it holds the alerts, entities, a timeline, comments, an owner, a severity and a status. In the Defender portal, Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents share one unified incident queue.

concepts.heading: Response: Automation Rules and Playbooks
concepts.body: Sentinel has two automation tools, and the exam likes to contrast them. Automation rules manage incident handling centrally: they can tag, assign or close incidents, change severity or status, add task lists for analysts, and run playbooks, all without writing a workflow. Playbooks are collections of response and remediation actions built on Azure Logic Apps, so they can use its connectors to act in other systems. Typical playbook uses are enrichment of an incident with extra data, opening and updating tickets in a system such as ServiceNow or Jira, posting to a Microsoft Teams channel, and response actions such as blocking a user account or isolating a machine. A playbook runs automatically when an automation rule triggers it, or manually from an alert or entity. Choose an automation rule for changes to the incident itself and a playbook for actions outside Sentinel.

concepts.heading: Hunting and Workbooks
concepts.body: Analytics rules wait for known patterns; threat hunting looks for attackers that no rule has caught yet. Sentinel offers hunting queries, many installed with Content hub solutions and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques, with result counts that suggest where to start. When an analyst finds suspicious rows, a bookmark keeps them together with the query, tags and notes, and a serious finding can be escalated to an incident. Notebooks support advanced analysis in Python, and a useful hunting query can become an analytics rule so it runs automatically. Workbooks are Sentinel's interactive dashboards, based on Azure Monitor workbooks: charts and tables built from queries over the logs, with templates that come with solutions. For example, a SOC manager can open a sign-in workbook to see failure trends, while an analyst hunts and bookmarks rare processes on two servers.

examPoints: A question that describes collecting, correlating and alerting on logs is testing SIEM, while one about playbooks, orchestration or automated response steps is testing SOAR.
A question that asks for tagging, assigning or closing incidents without another system is testing automation rules, while opening tickets or posting to Teams is testing Logic Apps playbooks.
A question that contrasts proactive searching with automatic detection is testing hunting queries and bookmarks versus analytics rules, and a dashboard need is testing workbooks.

quiz.q: A Microsoft Sentinel analyst wrote a hunting query that finds a rare attack technique. She now wants it to run on its own at regular intervals and raise alerts that become incidents. What should she do?
choices: Save its results as a bookmark so that Sentinel reruns the query every few hours
Add the query to a workbook so that its chart refreshes and alerts the SOC automatically
Attach the query to a playbook so Azure Logic Apps runs it when an incident opens
Create a scheduled analytics rule from the query with a lookback period and threshold
quiz.explain: Hunting is a manual, proactive search; to detect automatically, the query becomes a scheduled analytics rule, whose alerts Sentinel groups into incidents. Choice A is tempting because bookmarks keep hunting findings together with the query, but a bookmark preserves results for investigation and does not schedule anything.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly separates the SIEM side of Microsoft Sentinel from its SOAR side?
choices: SIEM runs playbooks in Azure Logic Apps, while SOAR collects logs through data connectors
SIEM collects and correlates data into alerts, while SOAR automates the response with playbooks
SIEM is used only in the Azure portal, while SOAR is used only in the Microsoft Defender portal
SIEM protects endpoints with antivirus, while SOAR protects email by scanning attachments
quiz.explain: The SIEM side ingests data through connectors, correlates it with analytics rules and creates alerts and incidents; the SOAR side responds with automation rules and playbooks. Choice A is tempting because both halves name real Sentinel features, but it swaps them between SIEM and SOAR.

days.recap: Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM and SOAR used in the Defender portal: connectors bring data in, analytics rules raise alerts grouped into incidents, automation rules and Logic Apps playbooks respond, hunting finds what rules miss, and workbooks visualize.

days.title: Defender XDR I: Incidents, the Defender Portal, Office 365, and Endpoint

concepts.heading: What Microsoft Defender XDR Is
concepts.body: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) looks only at devices. Extended detection and response (XDR) extends the same idea across many kinds of signal, so one attack can be followed from start to finish. Microsoft Defender XDR is a unified pre- and post-breach defense suite that coordinates detection, prevention, investigation and response across endpoints (Defender for Endpoint), identities (Defender for Identity and Microsoft Entra ID Protection), email and collaboration (Defender for Office 365) and cloud apps (Defender for Cloud Apps). Signals are shared between products: when Defender for Endpoint finds a malicious file on a laptop, Defender XDR can have Defender for Office 365 remove the same file from every mailbox, and the file is blocked across the suite. Defender XDR correlates signals only from the products the organization has licensed and provisioned.

concepts.heading: Incidents, Attack Disruption, and Hunting
concepts.body: An alert is a single signal that something suspicious happened, such as a malicious file detected on a device. An incident is a container of related alerts that tells the full story of an attack, even when the alerts come from different products or from external sources collected through Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud. Correlation engines build incidents automatically and keep adding evidence, so one analyst works the whole attack with its timeline, impacted users and devices, and evidence. Automatic attack disruption goes further: from high-confidence cross-product signals it contains an attack in progress by itself, for example by containing a device or disabling a user account, and the team can undo each action. Advanced hunting lets analysts write KQL, or use a guided builder, over about 30 days of raw data from the Defender products, and save queries as custom detection rules.

concepts.heading: The Microsoft Defender Portal
concepts.body: The Microsoft Defender portal is the central place for protection, detection, investigation and response across the Defender products. It brings together the incident and alert queues, advanced hunting, threat analytics, Microsoft Secure Score, and Microsoft Sentinel for unified security operations. Under Actions and submissions, the Action center lists actions taken on devices, users and other entities, manually or automatically, where they can be reviewed and undone, and Submissions let you send email, attachments, URLs, files or Teams messages to Microsoft for analysis when something was missed or wrongly blocked. Customers see only the features their subscription includes. Microsoft's own example: an organization with Defender for Office 365 but not Defender for Endpoint sees the email features but no device protection pages, so missing pages often point to a missing license.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Defender for Office 365
concepts.body: Email protection is a ladder. Built-in protection for all cloud mailboxes includes anti-malware, anti-spam, anti-phishing with spoof protection, quarantine and zero-hour auto purge (ZAP), which removes phishing, spam or malware messages after delivery when they are later found to be malicious. Plan 1 adds Safe Attachments, which opens attachments in a virtual environment (detonation) before delivery to catch unknown malware, Safe Links, which rewrites URLs and checks them again at the time of click in email, Teams and Office apps, and impersonation protection against look-alike senders posing as executives or partners. Plan 2 adds the tools of a security operations team: Threat Explorer, campaigns, automated investigation and response, and attack simulation training, which sends harmless phishing tests to staff and assigns training to users who click.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
concepts.body: An endpoint is any device that connects to the network. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is an enterprise platform to prevent, detect, investigate and respond to advanced threats on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS. Next-generation protection is Microsoft Defender Antivirus with ransomware prevention. Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules block risky behaviors that attacks rely on, such as Office apps creating child processes or scripts downloading files; Microsoft suggests testing many rules in audit mode first. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) uses a sensor that continuously records process activity, network connections, logons and file and registry changes, groups related alerts, and offers response actions such as isolating a device, running a scan or quarantining a file. Isolation cuts most network traffic but keeps the connection to Defender, so the investigation can continue.

examPoints: A question that describes alerts from email, devices and identities shown as one attack story is testing Defender XDR incidents, and one where Defender contains a device or account by itself is testing automatic attack disruption.
A question that separates protection before delivery, at the time of click and after delivery is testing Safe Attachments, Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge in Defender for Office 365.
A question about blocking risky behaviors such as Office apps starting child processes is testing attack surface reduction, while isolating a compromised device is testing EDR response actions.

quiz.q: A small company uses Exchange Online mailboxes but has not bought Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Which protection does it already have?
choices: Anti-malware and anti-spam filtering, with zero-hour auto purge of email
Safe Attachments, which opens every attachment in a sandbox before delivery
Safe Links, which rewrites URLs and checks them again each time a user clicks
Attack simulation training, which sends harmless phishing tests to all staff
quiz.explain: Every cloud mailbox gets built-in protection: anti-malware, anti-spam, anti-phishing with spoof protection, quarantine and zero-hour auto purge for email. Choice B is tempting because Safe Attachments is a well-known email protection, but it is part of Defender for Office 365 Plan 1, not the built-in layer.

quiz.q: An analyst investigating a Defender for Endpoint alert wants to see the processes, network connections and file changes recorded on a laptop before the alert fired. Which capability collects this data?
choices: Attack surface reduction rules, which block risky behaviors such as script downloads
Next-generation protection, which scans files with signatures and cloud intelligence
Endpoint detection and response, whose sensor records behavioral telemetry continuously
Defender Vulnerability Management, which inventories installed software and weaknesses
quiz.explain: The EDR sensor continuously collects behavioral telemetry such as processes, network connections, logons and file changes, which gives the analyst the timeline around an alert. Choice A is tempting because ASR is also part of Defender for Endpoint, but it prevents risky behaviors rather than recording what happened on the device.

days.recap: Defender XDR joins endpoint, identity, email and app signals into incidents in the Defender portal, with attack disruption and advanced hunting; Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Attachments, Safe Links and Plan 2 tools; Defender for Endpoint adds antivirus, ASR and EDR.

days.title: Defender XDR II: Cloud Apps, Identity, Vulnerability Management, and Threat Intelligence

concepts.heading: Defender for Cloud Apps as a CASB
concepts.body: A cloud access security broker (CASB) sits between users and cloud services. It gives visibility into which apps are used and lets the organization enforce security and compliance controls on those apps and their data, whatever the device or network. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps groups its features into four areas: fundamental CASB functionality, SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM), advanced threat protection as part of Defender XDR, and app-to-app protection.
